c0618: Zoning check before signing: restaurant use, Type I hood route, electrical service and seats
c0621: Ask the city planning (zoning) office whether the zoning allows a restaurant with a fryer and a griddle, whether the space can take a Type I hood with a duct up to the roof, what electrical service it has and what occupancy load it allows. Then ask the fire marshal in writing what the hood and fire suppression requirements are. With no exhaust path to the roof there is no tempura fryer or gyoza griddle, and the menu stays cold.
c0622: Decide your format before signing the lease: sushi bar + tables with take-out, or omakase counter
c0624: A sushi bar in view with tables, take-out and delivery (this plan: 40 seats in about 1,800 sq ft, or 167 sq m); take-out and delivery only in 450-650 sq ft (40-60 sq m); an omakase chef's counter of 10-12 seats by reservation; or a conveyor-belt (kaiten) or all-you-can-eat restaurant of 1,600-2,700 sq ft (150-250 sq m). Each one needs a different space, investment and margin.
c0625: Decide how you will meet the parasite rule: buy treated fish or freeze it yourself
c0627: Fish served raw must be frozen before service (FDA Food Code 3-402.11): at −4 °F (−20 °C) or below for 7 days, or at −31 °F (−35 °C) or below until solid and then held 15 hours, or until solid and then held at −4 °F for 24 hours. Tuna species are exempt, and so are feed-raised farmed fish such as salmon with a written statement from the supplier or the farmer. Your state adopts its own edition of the Code. If you freeze in-house, the freezer and its footprint go into the space plan.
c0636: Business license + sales tax permit (state and city)
c0638: Register with your state revenue department for a sales tax permit and with your city or county for a business license. Some states also ask for a separate food seller license. Rules, fees and timing vary by state, so confirm them with your CPA / bookkeeper before you open, and collect sales tax from your first sale.
c0650: General, product and liquor liability + property with refrigeration breakdown (spoilage) cover
c0653: Get quotes for general liability, product liability, liquor liability (beer, sake and wine), property and workers' comp. Tell the broker you serve raw fish and cook with a fryer, and ask about equipment breakdown and spoilage cover for the walk-in, the freezer and the sushi case.
c0659: Second-generation restaurant space of about 1,800 sq ft (167 sq m) with a route for the Type I hood
c0661: Room for a sushi bar in view with 10 stools and a 30-seat dining room, a kitchen, a walk-in, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and a to-go packing station by the door. A neighborhood with nightlife and weekend foot traffic.
c0662: Check the electrical service and the gas line for rice cookers, fryer, walk-in and sushi case
c0665: Gas rice cookers, fryer, griddle, fish refrigeration, freezer, hood and HVAC all draw power or gas. A service upgrade or a new meter takes time: ask the utility for the timeline and the cost.
c0670: The plan counts two months of rent before opening and a two-month security deposit. Ask for free rent while the sushi bar and the hood are being built.
c0671: Lease with restaurant use, hood rights and a beer & wine license contingency
c0674: It should name restaurant use and allow the sushi bar, walk-in and roof duct work. Ask your attorney for a contingency in case the beer & wine license is delayed or denied.
c0675: Architect / MEP drawings and plan review submittal
c0678: Layout of the sushi bar and the kitchen, electrical load, seats, ventilation, accessibility (ADA) and the hood duct to the roof. Ask your city for its mechanical and fire code requirements and which drawings the building department wants stamped.
c0681: Whether the space needs a conditional use permit or a change of use depends on your city's zoning code. Ask in the zoning check which approval applies and how long it takes.
c0685: Type I hood, UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air (permit and fire marshal sign-off)
c0688: Type I hood over the fryer, range and griddle, with a UL 300 fire suppression system and makeup air, installed under a mechanical permit and signed off by the fire marshal. Plan on cleaning it twice a year (NFPA 96, Table 11.4). A charcoal robata, if you ever add one, is a solid-fuel appliance that needs its own exhaust: ask the fire marshal first.
c0689: Build-out with smooth, cleanable surfaces (sushi bar, kitchen, dining room)
c0691: Sushi bar with a smooth, cleanable countertop, washable walls, non-slip flooring, cleanable ceilings, hand sinks near the sushi bar and in the kitchen, ADA restrooms and soundproofing if you have neighbors
c0692: Walk-in and a fish prep area separate from the cutting station
c0694: Whole fish is cleaned in an area with its own sink, away from the sushi bar cutting station and the hot line; the fish reach-in and the freezer sit next to the walk-in. Plan the flow: receiving, cold storage, cleaning, cutting, sushi bar.
c0696: Hot and cold water in the kitchen and at the sushi bar, drains with a grease interceptor (the fryer sends a lot of grease down) and HVAC for the dining room: the sushi case holds the neta (topping) worse when the room is hot
c0697: Hood over the fryer, range and griddle (ask whether the gas rice cookers go under it)
c0699: Hood with motor and grease filters covering the whole hot line, connected to the dedicated duct. Ask the installer for the airflow rate (CFM) and the filter cleaning schedule, and ask the mechanical inspector whether the gas rice cookers go under the hood.
c0700: To-go packing station by the door
c0701: A table with the boxes, soy sauce cups, chopsticks and bags, the ticket printer and the marketplace tablets, so drivers never cross the dining room or enter the kitchen
c0705: The final electrical, fire and building inspection sign-offs, and the certificate of occupancy. Keep copies: the health department, your insurer and your lender may ask for them.
c0708: Buy NSF-listed equipment: freezer (−4 °F or colder) with temperature logger, refrigerated sushi case and gas rice cookers
c0710: Ask for the freezer's data sheet: it must reach −4 °F (−20 °C) or colder in the product and log the temperature. In this kit it mainly holds fish that you bought already treated; freezing raw fish yourself for 7 days at −4 °F takes a lot of freezer space. The sushi case should hold the neta at 41 °F (5 °C) or below with a full dining room; size the rice cookers to your batches.
c0715: Written food safety plan with raw-fish (parasite) and sushi-rice controls
c0718: Fish served raw or nearly raw (nigiri, sashimi, maki, tartare, poke) must be frozen per Food Code 3-402.11: −4 °F (−20 °C) or below for 7 days, or the −31 °F (−35 °C) options. Tuna species are exempt, and so are feed-raised farmed fish such as salmon with a written supplier statement. For wild fish, farmed yellowtail (hamachi), mackerel (saba) and squid, get the supplier's letter or keep your own freezing log.
c0719: Freezing log by lot, kept 90 days, if you freeze in-house
c0722: Species, origin, lot, date and time in and out of the freezer, and temperature, for each lot you freeze yourself. Keep the log for 90 days after the fish is served (Food Code 3-402.12).
c0723: File supplier parasite letters and aquaculture statements (keep 90 days)
c0725: If the fish arrives already frozen for raw service, the supplier's letter must say so. For feed-raised farmed fish, such as farmed salmon, the exemption needs a written statement from the supplier or the farmer (3-402.12); for tuna, keep the invoice or letter that names the species. File them with the lot and keep them 90 days after the fish is served: the inspector asks for them first.
c0726: Consumer advisory (disclosure + reminder) on the menu, website and marketplace listings
c0727: Mark every raw or undercooked item with an asterisk or a description (disclosure) and add the reminder: "Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness" (Food Code 3-603.11). Put both on the menu, on your website and on every marketplace listing.
c0728: Fish held at 41 °F or below (32-34 °F in the reach-in); thaw under refrigeration
c0729: Hold fish at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, and keep the reach-in for the service fish at 32-34 °F (0-1 °C). Thaw in the walk-in, never at room temperature, and write down when it leaves the freezer. Vacuum-packed frozen fish labeled "keep frozen" (saku blocks often are) comes out of its bag before it thaws (Food Code 3-501.13).
c0730: Receiving log: reject tuna, yellowtail and mackerel above 40 °F
c0731: Measure and log the temperature of every delivery. Reject tuna, yellowtail (hamachi) and mackerel that arrive above 40 °F (4 °C): for these fish, the cold chain from receiving is the defense against scombrotoxin (histamine), which neither freezing nor cooking removes. For everything else, follow the limits in your food safety plan.
c0732: Decide TPHC or variance for sushi rice with your health department, in writing
c0733: Sushi rice is a TCS food, so there are two paths. (a) TPHC (Food Code 3-501.19): hold it up to 4 hours with the time marked on every batch and a written procedure, then discard it; this is the default in this kit. (b) A variance with a HACCP plan for acidified rice (3-502.11(C)): each county sets its own pH limit, and the health department decides. The kit sets no "legal" pH: get your choice in writing before opening.
c0734: If variance: pH of every batch with a calibrated pH meter, logged (TPHC: time-stamp every batch, discard at 4 h)
c0737: TPHC: write the time on every batch of rice and discard what is left at 4 hours, with no cooling and no reheating. Variance: measure and log the pH of every batch against the limit in your approved HACCP plan (the Food Code annex uses a critical limit below 4.2 as an example; your county sets its own). Calibrate the pH meter with its buffer solutions before you start.
c0738: Hot kitchen: gyoza, tempura and miso held at 135 °F or above; cool and reheat per Food Code
c0742: Lot and date of the fish, rice, nori and sauces, freezing logs and supplier letters, temperatures of the walk-in, the freezer and the sushi case, rice time or pH log, and the supplier of each ingredient
c0743: Recipe cards per piece with the major allergens (9 in the US)
c0744: Fish; crustacean shellfish (shrimp, crab); soy and the wheat in soy sauce (tamari only if its label says so); sesame (seeds, oil); egg (tamago, spicy mayo, tempura batter); milk (cream cheese); wheat in tempura and panko, and in imitation crab (starch, egg white: check the label). Mollusks (octopus, scallop) and mustard are not major allergens in the US, but guests ask. Read every label: they change by brand. The kit's calculator gives the cost of each piece.
c0746: Platters you pack before the customer orders, for the sushi case or for pickup, are prepackaged food: label them with the common name, ingredients with the major allergens, net quantity and your name and address (Food Code 3-602.11). Platters packed to order usually need less; ask your health department.
c0751: Use the higher of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour) and your state or local minimum for your lowest pay rate, and enter it in the "0. Assumptions" sheet. Servers are W-2 employees; their tips go on top of their pay and to the team, never to the owner or managers.
c0752: Hire the head sushi chef (itamae) and the sushi chef BEFORE the build-out
c0753: In this plan the owner is the GM, and the head sushi chef, who buys, cleans and cuts the fish, is a hire: the hardest one (the example plan pays about $30 per hour, a Kit estimate). Let both weigh in on the sushi bar and the refrigeration before you close the build-out: an absence of the only person who cuts closes the sushi bar.
c0759: Schedule for both services and for Friday and Saturday nights
c0761: Lunch and dinner Tuesday to Sunday, closed Mondays. On Friday and Saturday nights you need about six people: two at the sushi bar, one on the hot line, two in the dining room and one packing orders.
c0765: CFPM + food handler cards, with raw-fish handling
c0766: Have a Certified Food Protection Manager where your state requires one (Food Code 2-102.12), and food handler cards where your state or county asks for them. Add documented in-house training: hygiene, parasite freezing and supplier letters, sushi case temperatures, rice time or pH controls, major allergens and cross-contact.
c0767: Sushi bar training: cutting, ounces of neta and sushi rice per piece
c0768: Everyone at the sushi bar cuts and forms to the same weights: weigh 10 slices and 10 balls of sushi rice from each person and correct them. Neta and sushi rice that run heavy are the food cost that never shows up in the recipe costing.
c0771: Part of your duty to provide a safe workplace (OSHA): cuts from the sushi bar knives, burns from the fryer and griddle, slips on wet floors, cold exposure in the freezer and heavy lifting
c0777: Allergen matrix (9 major in the US) with fish, shellfish, sesame and the wheat in soy sauce
c0778: One row per piece and one column per allergen, with what is forgotten most: fish, shellfish, the sesame on inside-out rolls, the wheat in soy sauce and in imitation crab, and the egg in spicy mayo. Update it every time a supplier or a recipe changes.
c0781: A "gluten-free" claim has to meet 21 CFR 101.91 (under 20 ppm of gluten in the finished food). Soy sauce, tempura batter and panko contain wheat, and the fryer is shared. Disclose the wheat allergen and the cross-contact risk, and offer tamari only if its label says it is wheat-free, without promising anything.
c0784: Short menu (about 35 items) and lunch specials
c0786: Nigiri, sashimi, maki, hand rolls, classic and specialty rolls, platters of 12, 24 and 36 pieces, poke bowls, gyoza, edamame, miso soup and mochi, plus the midday lunch specials (bento or roll combos). A 60-item menu fills the sushi case with neta that gets thrown out.
c0787: Cost per piece and per platter by channel (calculator)
c0789: Use the Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator in the kit: the cost of each piece and the margin in the dining room, for take-out and on the marketplaces. Even with the higher marketplace price, a platter leaves about a fifth to a quarter less margin there than in the dining room.
c0790: Sales tax on the menu: one rate; check your state's to-go rules
c0792: The example uses a single sales tax rate. Some states tax to-go food differently from dine-in, and alcohol can carry its own rate: ask your CPA / bookkeeper, then set the POS and each marketplace up the same way.
c0793: To-go packaging that meets your local ordinances (some cities ban polystyrene)
c0794: Some cities and states restrict polystyrene foam, plastic straws and utensils unless the customer asks for them, so check your local ordinances before you order boxes. Ask your supplier which of your sushi trays, soy cups and bags comply.
c0795: Two fish suppliers with their parasite letters
c0796: One for salmon and another for tuna and the rest, or two for everything: with a single supplier, one bad week leaves you without a menu. Ask each one for the freezing or aquaculture letter, the delivery temperature and the price in writing: the plan estimates them.
c0797: Sushi rice, nori and sauces supplier with data sheets
c0798: Short or medium-grain sushi rice (price it by the 50 lb (23 kg) bag from a wholesaler), nori, rice vinegar, soy sauce and wasabi, each with its data sheet and its allergens
c0799: Fish seasonality and price alerts from your suppliers
c0800: Seasons change the price and the menu of the month. Ask each supplier for a seasonal outlook and price alerts, and re-cost the affected pieces in the calculator.
c0801: Marketplace contracts with a share cap
c0802: Read the commission (tiers vary by plan and zone on DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub), how often they pay out, who pays for promotions and what the tablet costs. Set a ceiling on the share of your sales you will let marketplaces take, and write it down.
c0804: Calculate the margin of each platter on the marketplace with its commission, the menu markup and the packaging; pickup at the restaurant pays no commission: push it. Tempura and gyoza travel badly: leave them off the delivery menu or use vented containers.
c0805: Allergens before ordering and cold chain for to-go (consumer advisory in the listing)
c0807: Show the major allergens and the consumer advisory in the online menu before the customer orders, on your site and on every marketplace listing. Pack raw fish in insulated bags with ice packs so it stays at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, including on marketplace deliveries.
c0808: Trademark search (USPTO), brand, photos and website with menu and allergens
c0811: Search the USPTO database first to check the name is not taken in your class (restaurant services). Real photos of the sushi bar and the pieces; a website with the menu, the allergens, the hours, pickup ordering and the privacy policy of each channel.
c0812: Google Business Profile, Yelp, Instagram and peak dates
c0813: Lunch and dinner hours, photos of the sushi bar and a reply to every review. On the calendar: Valentine's Day, Mother's Day and the New Year's Eve party platters, with pre-orders.
c0820: The plan starts in January, the slowest month, and the ramp-up runs from January to April; February, May and December are the peaks. That is why working capital matters. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
c0822: Cleaning plan for the sushi bar, the sushi case and the kitchen
c0823: Sushi case, color-coded cutting boards, knives, rice cookers and hangiri, fryer, griddle, hood filters and walk-in, each with its log
c0826: Several practice services to fine-tune the ounces of neta and sushi rice, the sushi bar timing and the packing of orders before you open
c0829: Walk-in, freezer, sushi case, rice time or pH log, hot holding for the gyoza and the cleaning sheet; fix any deviation before you serve
c0832: Freezing logs and supplier letters, rice time or pH logs, allergen sheets, traceability, temperatures, cleaning, training and pest control
c0833: Refrigeration, freezer and semiannual hood cleaning
c0836: A refrigeration technician checks that the freezer still reaches −4 °F (−20 °C) in the product; the hood and duct are cleaned at least twice a year (NFPA 96), and the grease interceptor is pumped on schedule.
c0839: With its calibration solutions, and logged: an uncalibrated pH meter passes sushi rice that is not safe. You only need it on the variance route.
c0840: Measure salmon yield and real ounces per piece, and recalculate (calculator)
c0842: Clean and weigh 3 whole salmon, weigh 10 slices and 10 balls of sushi rice, and enter the averages in the calculator; then compare your actual food cost (food purchases ÷ food sales for the month) with the plan's.
c0843: Schedule and stock for peak dates and holiday platters
c0845: December is the peak of the year, with holiday parties and New Year's Eve platters; February rises with Valentine's Day and May with Mother's Day and graduations; January is the valley. Prepare the schedule, the fish and the pre-orders early.
c0848: Sales, commission, promotions and packaging: if the marketplace share of your sales passes the ceiling you set, or its margin no longer covers the commission, trim the menu there or raise prices. Own drivers only as W-2 employees and only when the volume pays for them.
c0850: Covers per day, average check, food and labor against the Excel P&L; re-cost the menu whenever the price of salmon or tuna changes.
c0852: January opens the ramp and is the slowest month: look at each month's balance before a big payment
